hook.text: A man looked at two obviously different lines and said they were the same. He was not blind. He was conforming.

buildup.text: In Asch's 1951 study, actors unanimously gave wrong answers. The real subject sat among them, visibly uncomfortable.

discovery.text: 75% of subjects conformed at least once. They chose a clearly wrong answer just to match the group.

twist.text: One ally was enough to break the spell. A single dissenter cut conformity by 80%. Independence is contagious too.

climax.text: When a group unanimously agrees and you feel doubt, remember: one honest voice changes everything. Be that voice.

punchline.text: You don't need a majority. You just need one ally.

quiz.question: What reduced conformity most in Asch's experiments?
options: Telling subjects the correct answer beforehand
Having just one other person give the right answer

details.summary: Solomon Asch's 1951 experiment showed that people will give obviously wrong answers to conform with a group. About 75 percent of participants conformed at least once, demonstrating the powerful pull of social pressure even against clear evidence.
details.whyItMatters: Asch's work reveals that conformity is not about uncertainty but about social belonging. In economic contexts, this means consumers, investors, and employees often follow group behavior even when their own information says otherwise.
takeaways: 75 percent of participants conformed to clearly wrong group answers
Conformity persists even when the correct answer is obvious
Having even one ally dramatically reduces conformity pressure

faq.question: What exactly happened in Asch's line experiment?
faq.answer: Participants judged which of three lines matched a reference line. Confederates deliberately gave wrong answers. About 75 percent of real participants conformed to the group's wrong answer at least once, even though the correct answer was visually obvious.

faq.question: How does Asch's experiment apply to financial markets?
faq.answer: Investors conform to market consensus even when their own analysis disagrees. Analysts herd toward consensus estimates. Just as Asch's participants knew the answer but followed the group, investors often abandon sound analysis to match the crowd.
